---
title: "Part 1 — The four ideas"
---


No computers for this part. Ten minutes, and then you are allowed to let the
AI do the typing for the rest of your life.

## Idea 1: four places, three moves

Your work exists in four places. Git's commands are just moves between them.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["<b>Working directory</b><br/>the files you edit<br/>in RStudio"]
    B["<b>Staging area</b><br/>what will go into<br/>the next snapshot"]
    C["<b>Local repository</b><br/>your history<br/>on your laptop"]
    D[("<b>GitHub</b><br/>the shared history<br/>everyone sees")]

    A -->|"git add"| B
    B -->|"git commit"| C
    C -->|"git push"| D
    D -->|"git pull"| A
```

Three things to notice, because each one causes a specific student disaster:

1. **`commit` is local.** Committing does *not* put your work on GitHub. You
   can commit all week on a plane and nobody sees a thing.
2. **`push` is the only move that publishes.** Until you push, your teammates
   cannot see your work — and if your laptop dies, it is gone.
3. **`pull` is the only move that brings other people's work to you.** If you
   have not pulled today, you are working on yesterday's version of the project.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why is there a staging area at all?
So you can commit *some* of your changes and not others. You fixed a typo and
half-rewrote the model; you can commit the typo fix on its own. Most of the
time Claude will stage everything relevant and you will never think about it.
:::

## Idea 2: a commit is a labelled snapshot

A commit is the whole project at one moment, plus:

- who made it
- when
- **a message saying why**

The history is a chain of these snapshots. This is the entire reason git can
undo things: every previous state still exists.

The message is for a human — probably you, in five weeks, wondering why the
model changed. `"update"`, `"fixes"` and `"asdf"` are worthless. Good messages
say *why*, because the *what* is already visible in the diff:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Good
> Drop 3 participants with impossible ages — the export had -1 for missing
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Useless
> fixed data
:::

This is genuinely something Claude does better than most humans, so let it.

## Idea 3: a branch is a parallel line of work

A branch lets you build something half-finished without breaking the version
everyone else is using.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'gitGraph': {'rotateCommitLabel': false, 'showBranches': true}}}%%
gitGraph
    commit id: "setup"
    branch sex-table
    commit id: "your work"
    checkout main
    merge sex-table id: "PR #1"
    commit id: "next"
```

`main` is the branch that must always work. You do your work on a branch named
after what you are doing, then you **merge** it back into `main`.

A **Pull Request** (PR) is a merge with a conversation attached: it happens on
GitHub, your teammates can see exactly what changed, comment on it, and press
Merge. In this course the rule is: **you do not merge your own pull request.**
A teammate does. That single rule is the whole of code review.

## Idea 4: a conflict means git refuses to guess

If you change lines 40–43 of `report.qmd` and your teammate changes the same
lines, git cannot know which version is right. So it stops, puts both versions
in the file surrounded by markers, and tells you to decide:

``` text
<<<<<<< HEAD
Treatment was associated with a lower score than control (adjusted
difference -5.23, 95% CI -7.53 to -2.94).
=======
In this simulated dataset the treatment arm scored about 5 points lower
than control after adjustment for age and sex.
>>>>>>> de43b31
```

Read it as: *above `=======` is mine, below is theirs.*

::: {.callout-important}
## A conflict is not an error, and it is not the AI's decision

This is git protecting you. The alternative — a tool that silently picks one
version — would lose your work without telling you.

And notice what the example above actually is: two people who each said
something true that the other left out. The right answer is usually **both**,
rewritten. Claude can delete the markers for you in a second; only your group
knows what the paragraph is supposed to claim.
:::

## The napkin check

Before you touch a computer, on paper, without looking:

1. Draw the four places and label the three moves between them.
2. You committed your work this morning but your teammate cannot see it. Which
   move did you forget?
3. Your teammate says "it works on my machine" and you cannot reproduce it.
   Which move did *you* forget?
4. In your own words: what is a merge conflict, and who resolves it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
2. `push`. 3. `pull`. 4. Two people changed the same lines; git refuses to
choose; the humans who wrote them decide, then commit the decision.
:::
